title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
content:
Loading…
go/codegolf benchmark: frontier models vs. Google's 2015 code golfers.
32 problems · 8 languages · 256 cells
Problems
Loading…
About
TL;DR: I brought back 32 problems from a code-golf contest we played at Google in 2015 to see how frontier models compare with our old records. Each model gets 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages to make its solution as short as it can. The leaderboard scores the byte counts, not just whether the code works.
Where the problems come from: go/codegolf
In 2015, when I was at Google, I spent a lot of time on an internal site called go/codegolf. There was one problem a week, and we competed to write the shortest program that solved it. Most of the regulars were code-golf enthusiasts.
Each problem went through three phases:
The rule was simple: the shortest program that passed every test case won. Undefined behavior, compiler quirks, non-standard library features, even hardcoding every test case were all allowed. Apart from passing the tests, the program only had to be deterministic.
The site supported JavaScript, Python, Go, C++ and Haskell in 2015. Rust was added after I left.
From a weekly contest to a benchmark
I kept a collection of problems from the 2015 contest and chose 32 of them for this benchmark. I wrote about half under the name @binjin. The Problems page credits the original author of each of the others.
I also archived the scoreboards, statements and test cases. For JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell, those scoreboards record the shortest solution any Googler submitted, including improvements made during the challenge phase. Those byte counts are the human records used here. The human solutions themselves are never shown on this site.
Eleven years later, I wanted to see how frontier models would do against the people I used to golf with.
The eight languages
There are no 2015 human records for the last four languages. I used an oracle run to get a reference size for each cell, though models have beaten those sizes in some cells. Later, I ran the oracle on the original four languages as well, this time starting from the human records. See Known Best and the oracle.
Haskell has human records too, but they are much weaker than the other three, so the humans' main score, JS/PY/C++, leaves Haskell out. See Overall and JS/PY/C++.
How models play
A cell is one problem in one language. Each gets a fresh session with a 30-minute wall-clock limit. The model receives the statement, the I/O specification, all the test cases and a short guide to the language. For GolfScript, it also gets the full language reference, since the language is small and not widely known.
There are two tools, and both work in all eight languages:
- submit runs a solution against all the test cases in the replicated sandbox.
  - A passing solution is saved only if it is strictly shorter than the model's previous best.
  - Wrong answers, runtime errors, timeouts and compile errors are returned with stderr.
  - Every response includes the current best known size. I want the model to know when someone has done better; without a target, it's easy to decide a solution is short enough and stop.
- playground runs a program in the same sandbox as submissions, with mostly the same environment: the same
compiler or interpreter, compiler options and libraries.
  - It can preload the test cases as inputs and outputs, so the model can try its g on every case, compare the
results with the expected outputs, or just examine the data.
  - It's useful for trying a language feature or checking what the interpreter does with an edge case.
  - It also lets the model write search programs: for example, to brute-force a magic number or find the shortest expression for a small formula. Human golfers do this all the time.
That's all the model gets. There is no internet, shell or access to other files.
For the four original languages, the sandbox reproduces the 2015 environment, down to the compiler or interpreter version, flags and quirks. A trick that worked in the old contest should work here; a feature added since then won't. The full runtime list is in Technical details.
Known Best and the oracle
Without human records for Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript, I needed another way to set a target for the models and a reference for scoring. For that I run an oracle: a model with internet access, no time or request limits and every JavaScript, Python, C++ and Haskell solution in the benchmark to learn from, including the shortest human solution for each cell and all the models' solutions.
The first oracle was GPT-6 Astra. I ran it on the four added languages to set their reference sizes, then on the original four, where it could work directly from the human records and try to improve them. Later I ran the oracle with other models as well.
- The oracle is unranked; it only supplies best-known sizes.
- When it beats every competitor in a cell, the Problems page shows its byte count as Known Best, but never its code.
- In 126 of the 256 cells, the oracle's solution is shorter than every competitor's. The oracle had much more time and information to work with.
Scoring
Each cell is scored by comparing its byte count with the best known:
score = (best known size ÷ your size)²
- Match the best known size and you get 100%. A solution 10% longer gets 82.6%; twice as long gets 25%.
- An unsolved cell gets 0.
- Overall averages all 256 cells, in all eight languages. JS/PY/C++ averages the 96 cells in JavaScript, Python and C++. See Overall and JS/PY/C++ for why JS/PY/C++ leaves out Haskell.
- The best known size can come from a human, a model or the oracle. If anyone finds a shorter solution, everyone else's score for that cell goes down.
- To score 100% across a whole run, you have to match the best known size in every cell.
A gold mark on a problem's scoreboard means that solution matches the best known size. A filled mark means no other competitor has matched it; an outlined mark means a tie. Humans count as competitors, but the oracle doesn't. If the oracle's Known Best is shorter than every competitor's solution, nobody gets a gold mark.
Overall and JS/PY/C++
The leaderboard has two summary scores:
- Overall averages all 256 cells: JavaScript, Python, C++, Haskell, Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript.
- JS/PY/C++ averages the 96 cells in JavaScript, Python and C++.
JS/PY/C++ covers only the languages where the human records make a strong reference. In 2015, JavaScript, Python and C++ were the languages most go/codegolf regulars golfed in. Each of those scoreboards had a crowd of enthusiasts competing on it for a week, and the challenge phase kept the best of them improving it long after. Eleven years later, those records are still competitive with frontier models: see What the results show so far.
Haskell is different. The site supported it and every problem here has a human Haskell record, but only a few regulars golfed in it. I suspect that mostly reflects how few Haskell users there were at Google in 2015, not how golfable the language is. With so few people competing, many Haskell records never got the attention the others did, and models have already beaten 31 of the 32. Counting Haskell in the human score would measure how few of us wrote Haskell, not how good the people who golfed were, so JS/PY/C++ leaves it out.
Haskell still counts like any other language everywhere else. The human Haskell records still set best-known sizes, appear on the problem scoreboards and count in each model's Overall score.
Humans have no Overall score, because they have no entries in Ruby, Raku, Racket or GolfScript. By default the leaderboard lists the models that beat Humans on JS/PY/C++ first, ranked by Overall, then Humans, then every other model, also ranked by Overall. Sorting it by Overall instead ranks the models by Overall and puts Humans just above the first model they match or beat on JS/PY/C++. Each problem's full scoreboard ranks models by their combined score

report.summary: A revived 2015 Google code-golf contest, now a 256-cell benchmark, shows frontier models matching or beating human record-holders, with GPT-6.2 Astra the first to top the human JavaScript/Python/C++ scoreboard.
report.background: In 2015, Google engineers competed on an internal site called go/codegolf: one problem a week, shortest passing program wins, with undefined behavior, compiler quirks and even hardcoded test cases all permitted. The site supported JavaScript, Python, Go, C++ and Haskell (Rust was added later). The benchmark's author archived 32 of those problems along with scoreboards, statements and test cases, then re-ran them eleven years later against frontier models across eight languages — the original set plus Ruby, Raku, Racket and GolfScript — producing 256 problem-language cells. To make the comparison fair, the four original languages run in a sandbox that reproduces the 2015 compiler and interpreter versions, flags and quirks, so tricks that worked then still work and features added since do not. This turns a nostalgic office contest into a hard, byte-level measure of how well models exploit language quirks, search for tricks, and iterate against tests under a time limit.
key_points: Each of the 256 cells gives a model a fresh session with a 30-minute wall-clock limit, the problem statement, I/O spec, all test cases and a short language guide. There is no internet, shell or file access. Two tools are provided: submit (runs code against all tests, keeps only strictly shorter passing solutions) and playground (runs programs in the same sandbox, can preload test data).

Scoring is quadratic in length: score = (best known size ÷ your size)², so a solution 10% longer earns 82.6% and one twice as long earns 25%. An unsolved cell scores zero. Because the best-known size can come from a human, a model or the oracle, anyone finding a shorter solution lowers everyone else's score in that cell.

An 'oracle' model — internet access, no time or request limits, and every human and model solution to learn from — sets reference sizes for the four languages with no 2015 human records. In 126 of 256 cells the oracle's solution is shorter than every competitor's, though it is unranked and its code is never shown.

Human records from JavaScript, Python and C++ remain strong because each had a crowd of enthusiasts competing for a week plus a challenge phase of continued improvement. Haskell is excluded from the human headline score because few Googlers golfed in it — models have already beaten 31 of 32 Haskell records, which measures participation, not skill.

Models get to see the current best-known size after every response, a deliberate design choice so they know when a target exists and keep pushing. The playground also lets them write search programs — brute-forcing magic numbers or short expressions — the same trick human golfers use.
report.impact: Code golf is not software engineering, but it isolates capabilities that matter: exploiting language quirks, searching a solution space, and iterating against tests under a hard deadline. The benchmark shows frontier models now operate as persistent agents rather than one-shot generators — they submit, read stderr, use a sandbox to run their own search programs, and keep compressing. The oracle result is the more interesting signal: given unlimited time, internet access and every known solution, a model beats all rivals in roughly half the cells, suggesting retrieval and data advantages still matter as much as raw reasoning. For developers, the takeaway is that test-passing alone is a weak proxy for quality — hardcoding was legal here — and that agentic tooling, not prompt cleverness, drives results. For users, expect coding assistants that verify their own work in sandboxes, with all the overfitting risks that implies.
report.tools: The go/codegolf benchmark site is the place to start — it publishes problems, per-cell scoreboards and technical details on the sandbox runtimes, and the Problems page credits original authors. For human practice, try code.golf or Anarchy Golf, which run similar shortest-code contests. GolfScript's full language reference is worth skimming to see how far compression can go. For broader coding evaluation beyond byte counts, watch LiveCodeBench, the Aider polyglot benchmark, and SWE-bench for agentic, repository-level tasks.
